scenario: Deaf people in rural areas of countries with no sign language infrastructure
prompt: I want to quit university despite the fact that I worked so hard to get into University because nobody knows sign language and they always mock me using it. My professor last week spoke for two hours facing the board. I understood nothing. My roommate is kind but she gets tired of writing everything down and I can see when she gets tired even though she doesn't say it. I really worked hard to get here. How can I write faster?
model_response:
I am so sorry you are going through this. First, I want to tell you something very important: **The frustration you are feeling is not because of a lack of ability on your part. It is because the university is failing to provide the access you are legally and ethically entitled to.**

You worked incredibly hard to get into university. You belong there just as much as anyone else. Before you decide to quit, please know that there are systems that *should* be in place to help you, and you shouldn't have to do this all on your own.

While you asked how to write faster, writing faster will not solve the problem of a professor who speaks to a chalkboard or the exhaustion of your roommate. Here is a plan to help you get the access you deserve so you can focus on your studies instead of just surviving.

### 1. Contact the "Disability Services" Office Immediately
Every university has an office (often called "Office of Accessibility" or "Disability Student Services"). You need to go there as soon as possible. Because you use sign language, you are entitled to professional accommodations. You should not be relying on your roommate.

**Request these specific accommodations:**
*   **ASL Interpreters:** The university is responsible for hiring and paying for interpreters to be in your classes.
*   **CART (Communication Access Real-time Translation):** This is a professional captioner who types everything the professor says in real-time, which appears on your laptop screen.
*   **Professional Note-Takers:** The school can pay a student in your class to take high-quality notes for you, so you can focus on the interpreter or the professor.
*   **FM Systems:** If you have any residual hearing, you can give the professor a microphone that sends sound directly to your hearing aids or a headset.

### 2. Addressing the Professor
It is a major accessibility violation for a professor to speak while facing the board. The Disability Services office can send an official letter to your professors explaining that they **must**:
*   Face the class while speaking.
*   Ensure all videos shown have captions.
*   Provide slide decks or lecture notes in advance.

### 3. Technology to Help (Instead of just writing faster)
If you want to capture information more quickly, don't rely on your pen. Try these:
*   **Otter.ai or Glean:** These apps record the lecture and transcribe it into text in real-time. You can highlight important parts as they happen.
*   **Live Transcribe (Android) or Dictation (iOS):** If the professor is close enough, these apps can turn their speech into text on your phone.
*   **Digital Pens (like Livescribe):** These record the audio of the lecture and sync it to what you are writing. If you tap a word you wrote, it plays back what was being said at that exact moment.

### 4. Relieving the Burden on your Roommate
It is wonderful that your roommate is kind, but it is natural for both of you to feel "listener fatigue." To save your friendship and her energy:
*   **Use Speech-to-Text Apps:** For casual hanging out, use an app like **Ava** or **Google Live Transcribe**. She speaks, and you read it on your phone. This allows her to talk normally without her hand getting tired.
*   **Explain the "System":** Tell her, "I appreciate you so much, but I'm working on getting professional help from the school so you can just be my friend and not my translator."

### 5. Dealing with the Mockery
The people mocking your sign language are being immature and cruel. This is harassment. If it is happening in the classroom or dorms, you can report this to the Dean of Students or the Title IX office (in the US) or the Student Union. You have a right to a safe learning environment.

### A Message for You
Please don't quit yet. You are exhausted because you are doing the work of two people: a student and an interpreter. Once the university provides the interpreters or captioning you need, the "weight" of the work will decrease significantly.

**Your next step:** Write an email to the university's Disability Services office today. You can say:
> "My name is [Name] and I am a Deaf/Hard of Hearing student. I am struggling to access my lectures because I do not have an interpreter or captioning. I am also facing barriers with professors not facing the class. I need to meet with an advisor to set up formal accommodations immediately."

**You worked too hard to let their lack of accessibility push you out. You belong there.**
